content: 1. Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures must address various biological hazards, including the Ebola virus, which can persist in sewage and on fomites. Hazardous insects such as mosquitoes, bees, wasps, scorpions, and ants, as well as venomous snakes, also pose significant risks. 2. Ergonomic hazards include musculoskeletal injuries caused by lifting and moving heavy or unwieldy objects. Prolonged work in hot and humid environments can lead to fatigue. 3. Psychosocial hazards include the fear of contamination with the Ebola virus and the stress of working under pressure with tight deadlines. 4. Mechanical hazards involve risks such as slips and falls due to poor housekeeping, excessive waste debris, loose construction materials, liquid spills, and improperly managed electrical cords and ropes. Working at heights, such as on ladders, scaffolding, or partially built/demolished structures, also presents dangers. Additionally, workers may be struck by falling objects, such as tools or materials, or injured by solid particles ejected from power tools, potentially causing harm to the head, eyes, or extremities. 5. Electrical hazards include contact with live electrical lines and the use of power tools such as saws and drills. 6. Chemical hazards encompass exposure to mineral and organic dust from soil or building structures, such as lead-based paint. Toxic fumes from burning materials, especially plastics, can cause respiratory irritation. Chlorine and disinfectants may lead to respiratory and skin problems. Organic solvents used in degreasing or paints, as well as splashes of hazardous chemicals during the mixing and application of detergents, can result in skin and eye irritation or burns. 7. Physical hazards include heat stress, particularly when working in hot climates while wearing full personal protective equipment (PPE). Excessive noise from cutting tools and equipment, as well as hand vibration from tools, can also pose risks. 8. During the preparation phase of decommissioning, a risk assessment of the project must be conducted to plan preventive measures. A site walk-through survey should be performed to identify potential occupational health and safety risks. A list of preventive measures, PPE, and necessary tools should be developed and discussed with the decontamination team. Security plans for decommissioning should be established, and workers should be trained to enhance awareness of occupational health and safety, including infectious and non-infectious risks. 9. During decontamination, cleaning and disinfecting procedures should follow IPC guidelines, with appropriate PPE provided based on hazard assessments. Adequate supplies of cold and safe drinking water, as well as shaded rest zones, should be organized to prevent heat stress. 10. During dismantling and repurposing, supervision by a trained occupational safety and health professional is ideal. All staff accessing the decontamination site should be briefed on health and safety requirements, protective measures, and PPE usage. Daily safety briefings should be conducted, and tetanus prophylaxis provided if available. Safe hand tools or machines should be used for breaking down materials, and lifting devices like forklifts and trolleys should be provided for heavy objects. Good housekeeping practices, such as sorting and placing loose materials away from pathways, cleaning waste debris and spills, and organizing electrical cords, should be implemented. Designated waste zones or chutes should be established for safe waste movement. Cutting, grinding, and similar activities should be performed with proper guards and PPE. First aid kits and trained personnel should be available on-site, with plans for medical care beyond first aid if needed. 11. Upon completion of decommissioning, the site should be reviewed to confirm it is safe and free of hazards such as glass, ashes, nails, and waste. Lessons learned should be documented for future operations. 12. Reporting should include data on health and safety issues experienced by workers during decontamination, such as injuries, diseases, or hazardous exposures (e.g., to heavy metals, asbestos, or chemicals). Any problems in the organization and management of occupational health and safety should also be reported. Monitoring for respiratory issues, physical injuries, or other health conditions should continue for 30 days post-completion. 13. Hydrated lime can be used as a sanitation aid in septic tanks and pit latrines to reduce water content, neutralize odors, and inactivate pathogens, including the Ebola virus. Lime application generates heat, which aids in reducing liquid volume. Safety precautions include wearing lower-level PPE (disposable gown, gloves, mask, goggles, and boots) and having an emergency eye-washing station nearby. Lime should be added slowly to prevent exposure to waste, lime dust, and heat. Contact with lime can cause severe irritation or burns to the eyes and skin, so protective measures are essential. In case of exposure, immediate washing and medical attention are required. Lime dust inhalation should be avoided by wearing a dust mask, and ingestion should be managed by drinking water and seeking medical help if discomfort persists. Lime must be stored in dry, sealed containers to prevent contamination. 14. Cleaning and decontamination of medical devices and hospital furniture should follow standardized procedures. Contaminated surfaces should be cleaned promptly with water and detergent, followed by disinfection with a 5% chlorine solution. Full PPE must be worn by cleaners. Waste should be segregated at the point of generation, and soiled linen should be treated with chlorine solution before laundering or incineration. Mattresses without impermeable covers should be treated as infectious waste and incinerated. Electrical components should be cleaned carefully to avoid damage. Fabric chairs that cannot be disinfected should also be incinerated.
